title: Install Nessus on AlmaLinux 9
description: Let’s build your own Nessus 10.12.5 scanner on AlmaLinux 9, open its web page, and check that it is ready for the scanning class.
baseline: We’ll use VMware Workstation Pro, supported AlmaLinux 9 on a 64-bit Intel/AMD VM, and Nessus 10.12.5.
prerequisite: Before we start, let’s give Nessus its own practice computer inside VMware. That way you can learn without replacing Windows on your everyday PC. Here’s what we’ll use; the next lesson will help you check anything you’re missing. This scanner class uses a separate practice network. Keep the DC01/DC02 host-only VMnet2 lab separate; its blank gateway is not the scanner’s temporary internet setup.

lessons.title: Meet Your Vulnerability Scanner
lessons.description: First, let’s see what Nessus does and choose the practice computers you’ll use.
lessons.what: Think of Nessus as a building inspector for computers. It looks for known weak spots and gives us clues to investigate. It does not repair every problem for us.
lessons.why: When you understand what the scanner can and cannot tell you, you can make better decisions about what to fix. We’ll also make sure we check only the machines in your practice lab.
bestPractices: Write down the two target VMs you own or have permission to test, who is responsible for them, their addresses, the allowed scan time and who to contact if something goes wrong.
Keep the names straight: Nessus does the scanning. Tenable Security Center is a separate product for managing scanners and their results; we are not installing it here.
commonMistakes: Being able to reach a computer does not give us permission to scan it.
A finding means we need to check a possible weakness. It does not mean someone has already broken into the computer.

troubleshooting.problem: I’m not sure which computers I can scan.
troubleshooting.fix: Let’s settle that before using the tool. Get a written list from the lab owner or instructor, and use your private practice machines—not your employer’s network.

lessons.exercise: Explain Nessus to someone using the building-inspector example. Then write a short note naming the two computers you may test. Leave passwords out of the note.

quiz.question: What does a Nessus finding tell you?
options: A weakness may exist and needs review.
The host was definitely breached.
You may scan its whole network.
quiz.explanation: A finding contains saved result to assess; it does not prove a breach or grant permission.

quiz.question: What is Tenable Security Center?
options: A replacement name for AlmaLinux.
A separate platform that manages vulnerability information and scanners.
The RPM installer for Nessus.
quiz.explanation: Security Center and a Nessus scanner are different products.

steps.title: Name the job before using a tool
actions: On your Windows computer, open Notepad and save a private file named Nessus-Lab-Plan. This will be our notebook for the class.
Write: I will install one scanner, scan my permitted AlmaLinux and Windows practice VMs, fix one issue, and scan again.
Add one reminder: A scan gives me information to review; it does not automatically fix every problem.
steps.expected: Your notebook describes the order we’ll follow: scan, review, fix and check again.

screenshot.title: Name the job before using a tool — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: When you reach this point, take a screenshot of just your plan text. Leave out employer names, passwords and contact details.

steps.title: Draw the permission boundary
actions: Add three rows to your notebook: the Nessus scanner, the AlmaLinux target and the Windows target. A target is simply the computer we plan to inspect.
Write each VM’s name, its owner and when you may run the test. If you do not have an IP address yet, write not assigned yet instead of guessing.
Add our stop rule: stop the scan if a target becomes unstable or an unexpected address appears.
steps.expected: You have a short list of allowed machines and a clear reason to stop if the test goes off plan.

screenshot.title: Draw the permission boundary — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture your three-row machine list and stop rule using private practice names. Hide contact details.

steps.title: Separate the product names
actions: Open the official Get Started link below. We’re checking product names, not entering a license yet.
In your notebook, write Nessus scanner, Nessus Agent and Tenable Security Center. These names describe different jobs.
Mark our build as a standalone Nessus scanner. Use the scanner installer; do not use an Agent installer or change it to Security Center management.
steps.expected: Your notes identify the standalone scanner we are building, without adding a different management product.

screenshot.title: Separate the product names — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Take a screenshot of your product-comparison notes. We do not need a license or activation page in the picture.

lessons.pass: You’re ready to move on when your notes explain what Nessus does, how it differs from Security Center, and which private practice computers you may scan.
needs: You only need your Windows computer, Notepad and a place to save private lab notes for this first lesson.
Have the names or planned roles of your three practice machines: one scanner and two targets. It is fine to mark addresses as not assigned yet.

lessons.title: Check the Scanner Requirements
lessons.description: Let’s check your computer, installation files and license plan before we build the scanner.
lessons.what: We’re checking our ingredients before cooking: the right operating system, enough room to work and the correct Nessus installer.
lessons.why: Finding a missing file or a memory shortage now is much easier than diagnosing a half-finished installation later.
bestPractices: Choose a supported, patched AlmaLinux 9 release. Tenable’s current 10.12 table lists AlmaLinux 9.6 and later in the 9.x family; check the linked table if your image is different.
Start with a fresh VM for the scanner. Do not install over another Nessus Agent, Manager or scanner—installing can stop another nessusd process already on that machine.
Keep your private license and activation code in your approved password manager or other protected storage, outside GitHub and your class notes.
commonMistakes: The x86_64 installer is for a 64-bit Intel/AMD VM. It will not run in an ARM VM.
Nessus needs at least 30 GB beyond the operating system. Results and logs can keep growing, so that is not a promise that the whole VM needs only 30 GB.

troubleshooting.problem: My Windows computer cannot spare the resources.
troubleshooting.fix: Close or shut down other practice VMs and check again. If the host is still short of memory or disk space, use a more capable lab computer before continuing. Giving a VM more memory than the host can spare usually makes both slow.

lessons.exercise: Compare your plan with Tenable’s hardware and software tables. Write down the resources you can actually provide and the date you checked the requirements.

quiz.question: Which VM matches the supplied el9.x86_64 RPM?
options: An ARM AlmaLinux VM.
Any VM with a Linux logo.
A supported AlmaLinux 9 VM using x86_64.
quiz.explanation: EL9 identifies the compatible major family; x86_64 identifies the CPU architecture.

quiz.question: Can you commit your license file with the lessons?
options: No; keep it in private approved storage.
Yes, if the repository has screenshots.
Yes, if you rename it.
quiz.explanation: A renamed license is still sensitive.

steps.title: Check the supported operating system
actions: Open the Software Requirements link below in your browser.
Find the AlmaLinux row in the Nessus 10.12 table. Look for the supported 9.x versions and x86_64 architecture.
Write down the supported minor version you’ll install. For example, 9.6 is a minor version in the AlmaLinux 9 family. Recheck the table if your ISO is a different version.
steps.expected: Your notes name a supported AlmaLinux release and the Intel/AMD 64-bit image you plan to use.

screenshot.title: Check the supported operating system — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the public AlmaLinux support-table row with the documentation address visible.

steps.title: Reserve enough VM resources
steps.where: Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro and notes
actions: For our practice scanner, plan 4 virtual CPU cores and 8 GB RAM. CPU cores do the processing; RAM is the machine’s working space. Tenable lists 4 cores at 2 GHz, 4 GB RAM minimum and 8 GB recommended for a standard scanner.
Plan a new 80 GB virtual disk for this exercise. That gives the operating system, Nessus and its growing files room to work; Nessus itself needs at least 30 GB beyond the OS.

Check the physical Windows computer too. Leave it enough RAM, CPU and free disk space to keep running while the scanner and required target VMs are on. A growable virtual disk uses more real disk space as it fills.
steps.expected: You can explain how the scanner and target VMs fit on your host without using all of its resources.

screenshot.title: Reserve enough VM resources — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the VM resource plan and the Windows free-space view. Keep unrelated files out of the picture.

steps.title: Inventory the supplied files privately
actions: In File Explorer, put Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm in your private lab installers folder. An RPM is the Linux installation package. Check that Tenable supplied this scanner package, not NessusAgent.
Write down where it came from and the trusted vendor checksum—a long value used to check whether the file matches the original. Note that your license is available, but do not copy its contents.
Keep nessus-updates-10.12.5.tar.gz aside for now. Its name alone does not tell us whether it contains plugins or another update, and we still need to verify the matching signature.
steps.expected: You know which file installs Nessus. Your license stays private, and the update archive has not been used without checking it.

screenshot.title: Inventory the supplied files privately — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the RPM name and your non-secret origin/checksum note. Hide license files and private download addresses.

lessons.pass: You have a supported AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 image, a workable resource plan and a registration route your license supports.
needs: Open the official Tenable hardware and software links and your Windows storage/resource information.
Have your installer folder and license plan available; you can confirm that a private license exists without opening it for a screenshot.

lessons.title: Create the AlmaLinux Scanner VM
lessons.description: We’ll create a fresh AlmaLinux practice computer in VMware Workstation Pro.
lessons.what: Our new VM is called NESSUS-ALMA09. A VM is a computer running inside your Windows computer; this one will have its own Linux system and virtual disk.
lessons.why: Keeping Nessus on its own practice machine makes changes easier to understand and keeps them away from your everyday work.
bestPractices: Get the supported AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 ISO from the official AlmaLinux project. The ISO is the file we attach as an installation disc.
Use the private VMware NAT network from the lab-network lesson. NAT lets the VM use the planned network connection; do not bridge it onto an office network without permission.
Choose a new blank virtual disk for this VM. Leave physical disks and shared data disks alone.
commonMistakes: Use manual installation here. VMware Easy Install may skip choices we want to learn.
Keep the scanner and the Linux target separate. In the final scan lab, we need one scanner and two other target computers.

troubleshooting.problem: I don’t see the AlmaLinux installer.
troubleshooting.fix: Open this VM’s settings and check the ISO filename and Connect at power on. Then check its boot menu. We are fixing the VM’s virtual disc, not repartitioning the Windows computer.

lessons.exercise: Shut down and start your new VM once. Point out its virtual disk in VMware, then explain why it is different from your Windows system disk.

quiz.question: Which disk should the installer use?
options: The Windows host system disk.
A new blank virtual disk for this VM.
Any Western Digital disk attached to the host.
quiz.explanation: A separate virtual disk protects existing data.

quiz.question: Which machine runs these VMware wizard clicks?
options: The physical Windows host.
The Nessus browser page.
The future Linux scan target.
quiz.explanation: Workstation Pro runs on the physical host in this lab.

steps.title: Open the VMware creation wizard
steps.where: Physical Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro
actions: On your physical Windows computer, open VMware Workstation Pro and click File → New Virtual Machine.
Choose Typical, then Next. This gives us the standard wizard.

Choose I will install the operating system later → Next. Choose Linux and the closest supported Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 64-bit guest profile. AlmaLinux uses this compatible family for our VM settings.
steps.expected: The wizard is creating a new Linux VM. Your existing VMs have not been changed.

screenshot.title: Open the VMware creation wizard — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the actual VMware guest operating-system selection page. Keep unrelated VM names out of the picture.

steps.title: Give the scanner its resources
steps.where: Physical Windows host · Workstation VM wizard
actions: Name this VM NESSUS-ALMA09 and save it in your private lab folder so you can find it again.
Create a new 80 GB virtual disk. Choose the virtual disk option, not a physical disk.
Open Customize Hardware and give the VM 8 GB RAM and 4 total virtual CPU cores. Pause if your Windows host cannot spare those resources.
steps.expected: The VM summary shows NESSUS-ALMA09, the planned memory and CPU cores, and its new disk.

screenshot.title: Give the scanner its resources — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the VM hardware summary so we can read its memory, processors and disk size.

steps.title: Attach the installer and private network
steps.where: Physical Windows host · Workstation VM Settings
actions: Open CD/DVD → Use ISO image file → Browse. Choose your official supported AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 ISO and tick Connect at power on.
Open Network Adapter → Custom. Select the private NAT VMnet you recorded in the lab-network lesson; do not guess a different network.
Finish the wizard and power on the VM. We’re ready to install its operating system.
steps.expected: The AlmaLinux installer starts, and VMware shows the private network you intended to use.

screenshot.title: Attach the installer and private network — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the ISO and network settings, then the AlmaLinux boot screen. Use two genuine screenshots if one picture cannot show both.

steps.title: Install AlmaLinux on the new disk
actions: Choose Install AlmaLinux and your language. Open Installation Destination and check that only the new VM disk is selected before continuing.
Choose Server with GUI if you want the desktop and GNOME Terminal used in our examples. Nessus can also run on a dedicated minimal server, but its screen will look different.
Create a non-root user with administrator privileges. This is your everyday lab administrator; give it a strong password you keep privately. Finish installation and reboot.
If the installer starts again, disconnect the ISO. Sign in to AlmaLinux, open Activities → Terminal, and check that you are working inside NESSUS-ALMA09.
steps.expected: You are at the AlmaLinux desktop on NESSUS-ALMA09 and can open Terminal using your lab account.

screenshot.title: Install AlmaLinux on the new disk — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the finished AlmaLinux desktop and hostname view. Do not capture password entry.

lessons.pass: NESSUS-ALMA09 starts AlmaLinux from its own virtual disk, and you can sign in with your lab administrator account and open Terminal.
needs: Have VMware Workstation Pro and the official supported AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 ISO ready on Windows.
Make sure the host can spare 4 virtual CPU cores, 8 GB RAM and a new 80 GB virtual disk for this scanner, plus room for the other lab VMs.
Finish the private VMware network lesson first so you know which VMnet to select.

lessons.title: Set the Scanner Name and Network
lessons.description: Let’s give your scanner a recognizable name and an address that your Windows computer can reach.
lessons.what: We’re setting up the scanner’s address book and return address. Its hostname is its name; its IP address is where other computers reach it. DNS translates names into addresses.
lessons.why: The browser needs to find the right scanner. Online activation also needs working name lookup, a correct clock and the internet connection your lab allows.
bestPractices: Write down the current settings before changing them. Our sample addresses work only on a lab that really uses that address range.
Make network changes from the VM console—the VMware screen—so you still have a way in if an SSH connection drops.
Use the lab’s planned DNS and time servers. A machine that relies on Active Directory should keep using the domain’s DNS, not an unrelated public replacement.
commonMistakes: The VMware gateway and the Windows VMnet adapter are not necessarily the same address. Check both instead of guessing.
Giving Linux a hostname does not automatically add that name to a DNS server.

troubleshooting.problem: I changed the address and lost the connection.
troubleshooting.fix: Go back to the VMware console, reopen the same NetworkManager connection profile and restore the settings you wrote down. Also check that the VM’s network adapter still uses the planned VMnet.

lessons.exercise: Write a small address card for this scanner: name, IP, subnet prefix, gateway, DNS, Windows management address and Linux connection name. Explain what each item is for.

quiz.question: What should replace the sample gateway?
options: A random public DNS server.
The actual NAT gateway recorded for your private VMnet.
The scanner’s own IP in every lab.
quiz.explanation: The gateway must belong to your actual virtual network.

quiz.question: What does hostnamectl set-hostname do?
options: Creates a public DNS record.
Changes the VM CPU model.
Sets the local Linux machine name.
quiz.explanation: DNS registration is separate from setting the local hostname.

steps.title: Discover the current network first
actions: In the scanner’s Terminal, run the inspection commands below. These show the settings we already have; they do not change them.
Write down the active connection name, network interface, IPv4 address and default route. The default route points toward the gateway used to reach other networks.
On Windows, open PowerShell and run ipconfig. Find the adapter for this private VMnet and write down its IPv4 address; later we’ll use it as the allowed management source.
steps.command:
hostnamectl
nmcli connection show --active
ip -br address
ip route

breakdown.meaning: Shows the local hostname and system identity.
Lists active NetworkManager profiles; use the displayed connection name later.
Shows a brief list of interfaces and their assigned addresses.
Shows network routes and the default gateway.

steps.expected: You have the actual Linux and Windows network values in your notebook. Yours may differ from the examples.

screenshot.title: Discover the current network first — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the ip -br address and ip route results, showing only the private lab addresses we need.

steps.title: Set a clear scanner hostname
actions: Run the hostname command below to name the scanner nessus-alma09.
Run hostnamectl again and find Static hostname. It should now show the name you chose.
If you want to browse by this name, record how you will add a matching private DNS or hosts-file entry. Setting the Linux name does not publish that entry for you.
steps.command:
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname nessus-alma09
hostnamectl

breakdown.meaning: Asks Linux to run this one command with your permitted administrator rights. It may ask for your Linux password.
Changes the system’s local static hostname.
The course example name; use your approved unique name if different.

steps.expected: Static hostname shows nessus-alma09. If your Terminal prompt still uses the old name, close and reopen Terminal.

screenshot.title: Set a clear scanner hostname — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture hostnamectl showing the new name. Leave out anything unrelated to the lab.

steps.title: Apply the approved private address
actions: Read this example before running it. Replace Wired connection 1 and all four network values with your plan. Our example uses 192.168.77.0/24 and gateway 192.168.77.2; those are not universal settings.
Choose an unused scanner address. Use 192.168.77.30 only if your lab has reserved that address for this VM.
Apply the connection profile, then run ip -br address and ip route again. Keep the VMware console open while you check the result.
steps.command:
sudo nmcli connection modify 'Wired connection 1' ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.77.30/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.77.2 ipv4.dns 192.168.77.10
sudo nmcli connection up 'Wired connection 1'
ip -br address
ip route

breakdown.meaning: Edits a NetworkManager connection profile with administrator rights.
A quoted example profile name; replace it with the exact active name.
Uses the explicit static IPv4 settings.
Example unused scanner address with a 24-bit subnet prefix.
Sets the actual next-hop router for this network.
Sets the planned DNS resolver; these values are examples, not universal defaults.
Activates the modified profile and can briefly interrupt connectivity.

steps.expected: The interface shows your planned fixed IP address and gateway, and DNS uses your planned resolver.

screenshot.title: Apply the approved private address — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the resulting private IP address and route. Hide unrelated interfaces or private network information.

steps.title: Check DNS and the clock
actions: For an online scanner, run getent to check whether Linux can look up the documented plugin server name. Use the lab’s allowed proxy settings if your connection needs a proxy.
Run timedatectl and check the date, time zone and clock synchronization. A badly wrong clock can break secure connections.
If this scanner is deliberately offline, it cannot contact internet update services. Write down the offline route instead of trying to bypass the lab’s network rules.
steps.command:
getent hosts plugins.nessus.org
timedatectl

breakdown.meaning: Asks Linux’s configured name-lookup system to find addresses for the name that follows.
The documented Tenable plugin service hostname, not a scan target.
Shows the clock, time zone and synchronization state so you can check whether the VM has the right time.

steps.expected: For an online build, name lookup gives an address and the clock is correct and synchronized. For an offline build, your notes clearly identify the offline activation plan.

screenshot.title: Check DNS and the clock — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the useful DNS and clock results. Keep proxy passwords out of every screenshot.

lessons.pass: The scanner has the name and address you planned, and you can explain how your Windows computer reaches it. Name lookup works where your online or offline plan requires it.
needs: Start NESSUS-ALMA09 and open its screen directly in VMware. Keep that console open while changing network settings.
Have the actual private VMnet address range, gateway, DNS server and Windows adapter address in your notebook. Do not borrow sample addresses unless they really match your lab.

lessons.title: Copy the RPM from Windows
lessons.description: We’ll copy the Nessus installer from Windows into your Linux home folder.
lessons.what: SCP is a secure delivery tool. It carries the RPM through SSH, the encrypted connection between your Windows computer and the Linux scanner.
lessons.why: Before we install anything, let’s make sure the right file arrived on the right computer without being changed.
bestPractices: On the first connection, compare the scanner’s SSH fingerprint with the one shown through its VM console. The fingerprint helps us recognize the machine we meant to reach.
For this step, copy only the installer. Keep your license files separate and private.
commonMistakes: A path beginning C:\ is on Windows. Do not type that Windows path into the Linux shell.
Replace the sample Linux account with an account that already exists and is allowed to sign in.

troubleshooting.problem: SCP waits and eventually times out.
troubleshooting.fix: Check that sshd is running in AlmaLinux, that the private network is correct and that TCP 22 is allowed from your Windows management computer. Then check the scanner IP you entered.

lessons.exercise: Point to each part of the SCP command and explain it: the Windows file, the Linux username, the scanner address and the destination folder.

quiz.question: Where do you type the scp command in this lesson?
options: The Nessus activation form.
Windows PowerShell on the physical host.
The AlmaLinux installer partition screen.
quiz.explanation: The file starts on Windows, so this command is run there.

quiz.question: What does a matching checksum establish?
options: The file matches a trusted reference value, if that value came from the vendor.
The license allows unlimited scanning.
The scanner is already installed.
quiz.explanation: A checksum needs a trusted comparison value; it does not activate software.

steps.title: Prepare the encrypted transfer path
actions: At the scanner’s VM console, use the commands below to check the SSH service. SSH lets us securely sign in and transfer files.
If openssh-server is missing, install it from the lab’s approved AlmaLinux repositories, then start sshd as shown.
Keep SSH access limited to your Windows management address through the private-lab firewall plan. We do not need to expose SSH to the public internet.

Use the VM console to display the scanner’s SSH public host-key fingerprint. If the first SCP prompt says ED25519, compare its SHA-256 fingerprint with that ED25519 public host key. If it names another algorithm, check that matching public host key. Stop on a mismatch you cannot explain.
steps.command:
sudo dnf install openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd
sudo systemctl status sshd --no-pager
sudo ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

breakdown.meaning: Installs AlmaLinux’s SSH server package from configured repositories.
Starts SSH now and enables it after reboot.
Keeps the result in your normal Terminal window instead of opening a separate scrollable viewer.
Displays a key fingerprint; -l lists the fingerprint and -f chooses the key file.
The server’s ED25519 public host key. Compare the same algorithm; never display or copy the private file without .pub.

steps.expected: The SSH service is available to your permitted Windows management computer, and you have a trusted way to recognize its host key.

screenshot.title: Prepare the encrypted transfer path — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the sshd status. Do not show private keys or unrelated public addresses.

steps.title: Copy the RPM from your Windows host
actions: Back on the physical Windows computer, open PowerShell. Change the example Windows file path, Linux account and scanner IP to the values in your notes.
Run scp. If this is your first connection, compare the fingerprint with the VM console before you accept it.
If asked for the Linux account password, type it privately and press Enter. Seeing no characters while typing is normal. Do not paste the password into SONIC-Academy.
steps.command: scp "C:\SONIC-Lab\Installers\Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm" labadmin@192.168.77.30:~/

breakdown.meaning: Copies a file over SSH.
The quoted source file on Windows; replace this with its real path.
Example existing Linux user and scanner address.
Copies into that remote user’s home directory.

steps.expected: SCP finishes without an error and you are back at the Windows PowerShell prompt.

screenshot.title: Copy the RPM from your Windows host — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the RPM filename and completed transfer only. Leave out passwords and unrelated machine details.

steps.title: Compare the transferred file
actions: Return to Terminal on NESSUS-ALMA09. List the RPM and calculate its hash with the commands below.
Compare the entire hash—not just the first few characters—with the trusted Tenable value and the source file’s hash on Windows.
If the filename, size or hash is not what you expected, stop here. We’ll sort out the file before letting an installer change the VM.
steps.command:
ls -lh ~/Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm
sha256sum ~/Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm

breakdown.meaning: Lists the file with details and a readable size.
Your current Linux account’s home directory.
Calculates the file’s SHA-256 fingerprint; compare every character, not just its beginning.

steps.expected: The correct RPM is present, and its whole hash agrees with the trusted source.

screenshot.title: Compare the transferred file — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the RPM listing and hash comparison. Keep license files out of the view.

lessons.pass: The RPM is in your Linux account’s home folder, and its full SHA-256 hash matches the trusted installer value.
needs: Have the verified Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm file on Windows and its trusted vendor checksum to compare.
Start your AlmaLinux scanner, know its private address and have a permitted Linux sign-in account.
Open the scanner’s VMware console as well as Windows PowerShell so you can check the SSH host fingerprint before accepting it.

lessons.title: Install the Nessus RPM
lessons.description: Now that the file checks out, let’s install Nessus with AlmaLinux’s package manager.
lessons.what: dnf is the package manager: it puts the application files in the right places and keeps a record of what was installed.
lessons.why: Using the package manager lets us check the installed version later and see any missing supporting packages before we continue.
bestPractices: Use the verified EL9 x86_64 scanner RPM from our earlier check. A similarly named Nessus Agent package does a different job.
Keep /opt/nessus as a real supported directory, not a symbolic link pointing somewhere else. Read any signature or required connection or service error before proceeding.
commonMistakes: Do not force the install with --nogpgcheck, --nodeps or an installer from a random mirror. Those shortcuts hide checks we need.
Copying the RPM into Linux delivered the installer; it did not install Nessus yet.

troubleshooting.problem: dnf reports a signature or required connection or service error.
troubleshooting.fix: Read the whole error with your instructor. Recheck the file’s trusted source and the configured AlmaLinux repositories, then resolve the correct package or trusted-key requirement. Do not bypass the failed check.

lessons.exercise: Show the downloaded RPM, the installed package record and the Nessus administration tool. Explain how an installer file differs from the application it installs.

quiz.question: Why does the install command include ./?
options: It means reboot.
It identifies a local file in the current directory.
It bypasses the firewall.
quiz.explanation: The local path tells dnf to use the file you copied.

quiz.question: What should you do with an unexpected signature error?
options: Force the install with verification disabled.
Delete all firewall rules.
Stop and verify the file, repository and trusted signing material.
quiz.explanation: Investigate authenticity and configuration before proceeding.

steps.title: Inspect before installing
actions: Open Terminal in the scanner and change to your home folder, where we copied the verified RPM.
Run the inspection commands to read the RPM’s details and check the machine’s CPU architecture again.
Look for version 10.12.5 and x86_64. These details tell us what the package claims to contain; they do not replace the trusted hash comparison we already made.
steps.command:
cd ~
uname -m
rpm -qip ./Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm

breakdown.meaning: Moves into your Linux home directory.
Shows the machine architecture.
Queries information about a package file; -q queries, -i displays information, and -p selects a file.
The local scanner RPM in the current directory.

steps.expected: The package details match the version and architecture we planned to install.

screenshot.title: Inspect before installing — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the package name, version, architecture and uname result. Keep other personal files out of the view.

steps.title: Install with dnf
actions: Run the dnf install command below, then pause to read the proposed changes before answering its confirmation question.
Confirm that it lists the expected Nessus package and only legitimate supporting packages from the lab’s approved repositories.
Let dnf finish and return you to the prompt. Save the result you actually get; if it reports an error, we’ll diagnose it before moving on.
steps.command: sudo dnf install ./Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm

breakdown.meaning: Asks Linux to run this one command with your permitted administrator rights. It may ask for your Linux password.
Installs software and resolves required connections and services through configured repositories.
Uses this exact local EL9 x86_64 package, rather than searching for a different product.

steps.expected: dnf finishes without an unresolved error and adds Nessus to the installed package record.

screenshot.title: Install with dnf — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the actual transaction summary and final result. Hide any proxy credentials.

steps.title: Check the installed version
actions: Run the package query below to ask Linux which Nessus version is now installed.
Check that /opt/nessus/sbin/nessuscli exists. This is the tool we’ll use for some Nessus administration tasks.
We have installed the files, but we are not ready to scan yet. Next we’ll start the service, set up access and initialize plugins.
steps.command:
rpm -q Nessus
ls -l /opt/nessus/sbin/nessuscli

breakdown.meaning: Asks the installed-package record which Nessus version is on this machine.
Shows details of the specified installed file.
The Linux Nessus administration utility; this is an installed executable, not the original RPM.

steps.expected: rpm identifies the installed Nessus version, and the Nessus administration file is present under /opt/nessus/sbin.

screenshot.title: Check the installed version — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture your real package query and tool path. We want your result, not a copied example of success.

lessons.pass: The package record identifies Nessus 10.12.5 for the intended architecture, and the Nessus administration tool exists at its installed path.
needs: Finish the file-transfer lesson so the verified RPM is in your Linux home folder.
Open Terminal on NESSUS-ALMA09 using an account that may run sudo. Have access to the approved package repositories or offline required connection or service plan.

lessons.title: Start and Manage nessusd
lessons.description: Let’s start Nessus, check its background service and practice one careful restart.
lessons.what: An application can keep working in the background even when no window is open. On Linux, the Nessus background service is named nessusd.
lessons.why: The browser page needs this service. If the service is stopped, changing browser or firewall settings will not start it for us.
bestPractices: Before stopping or restarting a scanner beyond this fresh lab, check that nobody has a scan running.
Use systemctl to manage the Linux service. Use Nessus’s own scan controls to start or stop an individual scan.
commonMistakes: enable sets the service to start at boot. By itself, it does not necessarily start the service immediately; that is why our command also uses --now.
A running service is one good sign. Activation and plugin loading still need their own checks.

troubleshooting.fix: Read the status and journal messages before trying another restart. Check disk space and installation errors so we fix the cause instead of repeatedly interrupting the service.

lessons.exercise: On this fresh scanner, before any scans exist, practice the controlled restart shown below. Explain which check tells you about startup after reboot and which tells you about right now.

quiz.question: What does enable --now do?
options: Enables startup and starts the service now.
Starts one vulnerability scan.
Registers a license.
quiz.explanation: enable sets boot behavior; --now also starts it immediately.

quiz.question: What does listening on TCP 8834 prove?
options: Every target is patched.
A process is accepting connections on that port.
Every plugin is initialized.
quiz.explanation: A listener is one check; browser activation and plugin readiness are separate.

steps.title: Start and enable the service
actions: Run the first command to start Nessus now and arrange for it to start after a reboot.
Run the next two checks separately. One asks whether startup is enabled; the other asks whether Nessus is running right now.
If the current state is failed or inactive, pause and use the troubleshooting lesson. There is no need to rush past a service that has not started.
steps.command:
sudo systemctl enable --now nessusd
systemctl is-enabled nessusd
systemctl is-active nessusd

breakdown.meaning: Lets you ask about or manage a Linux background service. Think of it as the service control panel in Terminal.
Sets Nessus to start after boot and also starts it now, so we do not have to run a separate start command.
The Linux service name for Nessus. Use this exact spelling when asking systemctl about it.
The first asks whether Nessus starts at boot; the second asks whether it is running right now.

steps.expected: For a successful fresh installation, the checks report enabled and active. Use the result on your own screen.

screenshot.title: Start and enable the service — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture your systemctl checks with the nessusd service name and their actual results.

steps.title: Read the service and port state
actions: Read the service summary from systemctl status. Look for its current state and any error message.
Run the ss command to check whether an application is listening locally on TCP port 8834. A listening port is a place where the service can accept connections.
If no listener appears yet, give startup a little time and check the logs. Opening more firewall ports cannot fix a service that is not listening.
steps.command:
sudo systemctl status nessusd --no-pager
sudo ss -lntp 'sport = :8834'

breakdown.meaning: Keeps the result in your normal Terminal window instead of opening a separate scrollable viewer.
Shows listening (-l), numeric (-n), TCP (-t) sockets and their process (-p).
Filters to local source/listening port 8834.

steps.expected: Nessus is running, and ss shows the expected listener on its local address and port.

screenshot.title: Read the service and port state — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the service summary and TCP 8834 listener. Leave out unrelated network connections.

steps.title: Practice a controlled service restart
actions: Confirm that this new lab scanner has no scans running. A restart would interrupt them.
Run the restart command once, then check the service state again.
Notice that browser access may briefly stop while Nessus restarts. Treat a restart as a planned interruption, not a cure for every problem.
steps.command:
sudo systemctl restart nessusd
systemctl is-active nessusd

breakdown.meaning: Stops and starts the service. Expect a short interruption, so check for active scans first.
Asks whether the service is running at this moment; it does not start a stopped service.

steps.expected: The service returns to active, and its expected listener appears again.

screenshot.title: Practice a controlled service restart — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the restart command and the service’s final state. We do not need any license information.

lessons.pass: You have checked that nessusd will start at boot, is running now and has a listener for the Nessus HTTPS port.
needs: Finish the RPM installation and stay in Terminal on NESSUS-ALMA09.
Use your permitted sudo account. This should still be a fresh scanner with no scans running while we practice a restart.

lessons.title: Allow Private HTTPS Access
lessons.description: We’ll let your Windows management computer open the Nessus page without opening it to everyone.
lessons.what: Think of the firewall as a door guard. We’ll allow one computer through one door: the Nessus HTTPS port, TCP 8834.
lessons.why: This web page controls the scanner and may contain sensitive reports. It should be reachable only from the places you intend to manage it.
bestPractices: Use the zone connected to the real VM interface and the actual Windows management adapter address. A firewalld zone is a named set of network rules.
Keep these jobs separate: this rule lets your browser reach Nessus; other rules control updates leaving the scanner and traffic between the scanner and its targets.
commonMistakes: Opening 8834 does not also open SSH or Windows SMB. Each service has its own connection needs.
Do not use the NAT gateway address just because it looks familiar. The allowed source must match the Windows computer making the connection.

troubleshooting.problem: The rule is there, but Windows still times out.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the active interface’s zone, compare the allowed source with Windows’ actual VMnet address, and check that Nessus is listening. A correct rule in the wrong zone will not help this connection.

lessons.exercise: Explain the difference between letting one management address reach port 8834 and letting every address reach it. Show which choice your rule makes.

quiz.question: Which source address belongs in this management rule?
options: Any public address found online.
The actual approved Windows management source IP.
The scanner’s loopback address in all labs.
quiz.explanation: Match the connecting management computer’s real address.

quiz.question: Does opening inbound 8834 give scan permission for all targets?
options: Yes.
Only if the scanner is Linux.
No; scope and target access are separate.
quiz.explanation: A web-console rule does not grant authorization or configure all scan paths.

steps.title: Find the active firewalld zone
actions: In the scanner Terminal, run the two inspection commands below to check whether firewalld is running and which zones are in use.
Find the zone attached to the interface your Windows computer uses to reach this VM.
Write down that zone name. Our next example uses public; if yours is different, use your actual zone instead.
steps.command:
sudo firewall-cmd --state
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones

breakdown.meaning: The Terminal tool we use to check or change firewalld, AlmaLinux’s network door guard.
Asks whether the firewall service is running, without changing its rules.
Shows which named firewall rule sets are attached to the current network interfaces or sources.

steps.expected: firewalld is running, and you can point to the zone used by the scanner’s active interface.

screenshot.title: Find the active firewalld zone — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the firewalld state and the zone/interface mapping we need for this step.

steps.title: Add the source-limited web rule
actions: Before running this example, replace public with your actual zone and 192.168.77.1/32 with your Windows management IP followed by /32. The /32 means one IPv4 address.
Add the permanent rule, then reload firewalld so the saved rule is used by the running firewall.
We do not need a router port-forward or a public allow-from-everywhere rule for this private exercise.

Read the full zone rules too. An existing broad 8834 allowance or a trusted/accept-all zone can still let other computers through. Ask the lab owner to approve any correction; adding a narrow rule does not remove an older broad one.
steps.command:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.77.1/32" port port="8834" protocol="tcp" accept'
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-rich-rules
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all

breakdown.meaning: Saves the rule so it will still be there after firewalld restarts.
Example active zone; replace it with your recorded zone.
Adds a rule containing source and port conditions.
Makes this an IPv4 rule; IPv6 needs its own approved design.
Example single management host; /32 matches one IPv4 address.
Allows the Nessus HTTPS management port for that source.
Makes the running firewall use its saved permanent rules.
Shows the detailed rules in the selected zone so you can check the source and port.
Shows the zone’s services, ports, sources and rich rules so you can spot a broader allowance. Replace public with the actual reviewed zone.

steps.expected: The intended Windows source can reach TCP 8834 after the reload. You have also checked the other zone rules that still apply.

screenshot.title: Add the source-limited web rule — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the rule using private training values and the resulting firewall listing. Hide unrelated addresses.

steps.title: Test the port from Windows
actions: On the physical Windows computer, open PowerShell and use your scanner’s recorded private IP in the example.
Run Test-NetConnection and find TcpTestSucceeded. This checks the TCP connection to 8834, not just whether the computer answers a ping.
If it says False, work back through the service, listener, source rule and VMnet route, in that order.
steps.command: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 192.168.77.30 -Port 8834

breakdown.meaning: A Windows PowerShell tool that checks whether your computer can make a network connection.
Names the scanner’s private IP address or a hostname that your computer can look up.
Checks the TCP port used by the Nessus HTTPS page. This is different from a ping test.

steps.expected: TcpTestSucceeded reads True when this Windows computer can make the intended TCP connection to the scanner.

screenshot.title: Test the port from Windows — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture Test-NetConnection for your private scanner address. Keep other network interfaces out of the view.

lessons.pass: The active network zone has the intended TCP 8834 rule for your permitted Windows management address, and you have reviewed wider rules that could override the restriction.
needs: Have the scanner’s private address and your Windows management adapter’s actual address in your notebook.
Check that nessusd is running and listening on TCP 8834 before changing a firewall rule.
Open AlmaLinux Terminal and Windows PowerShell; we’ll make the rule in Linux and test it from Windows.

lessons.title: Open the Nessus Web Console
lessons.description: Let’s open the Nessus page in your browser and check that it belongs to your scanner.
lessons.what: The scanner is running inside AlmaLinux. Your Windows browser is just the window you use to manage it.
lessons.why: We want to recognize our own scanner before entering a private activation code or password into any page.
bestPractices: Use the private HTTPS address you recorded. Check the certificate and target before making any temporary browser exception in this controlled lab.
For ongoing use, arrange a trusted certificate through the approved process. The lesson is not asking you to ignore warnings on other websites.
commonMistakes: localhost means the computer running the browser. In a Windows browser, it means Windows—not your AlmaLinux VM.
Type https:// and the :8834 port. Plain http:// asks for a different kind of connection.

troubleshooting.fix: Return to the Windows port test. Does it time out, refuse the connection or show a certificate warning? Those are different clues, so identify the one you have before changing settings.

lessons.exercise: Write the address you would use in a browser inside the scanner VM, then the address you use on Windows. Explain why they can differ.

quiz.question: Which Windows-host URL reaches the Alma scanner?
options: https://localhost:8834 in every case.
https:// followed by the scanner private IP and :8834.
quiz.explanation: localhost on Windows refers to Windows; use the scanner’s address.

quiz.question: What should you do before entering secrets into a warning page?
options: Verify the target and certificate through your controlled lab.
Disable browser certificate checks globally.
Send the password to the academy.
quiz.explanation: A lab self-signed certificate still requires target verification.

steps.title: Build the correct URL
actions: Look up the scanner’s actual private IP in your notebook.
In your Windows browser, type https://192.168.77.30:8834, replacing the sample address with your scanner’s address.
Do not use localhost in this Windows browser. That name would point back to Windows unless you were browsing from inside the scanner VM.
steps.expected: The browser reaches Nessus or shows a certificate warning for the exact private address you entered.

screenshot.title: Build the correct URL — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the address bar and the warning or welcome page. Keep credentials out of the picture.

steps.title: Inspect the lab certificate
steps.where: Physical Windows host · browser certificate viewer
actions: Use the warning page or browser site-information button to open certificate details. The exact button wording depends on your browser.
Compare the address and certificate identity or fingerprint with your scanner console or a trusted lab record. We are checking which machine answered.
Only for this confirmed private lab, use your browser’s Advanced/Continue option if the lab policy permits it. Stop if the address or fingerprint is unexpected.
steps.expected: You understand that the first certificate is self-signed and have checked that the connection is to your intended scanner.

screenshot.title: Inspect the lab certificate — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture your scanner’s non-secret certificate subject, issuer and fingerprint details.

steps.title: Identify the actual Nessus page
steps.where: Physical Windows host · Nessus welcome page
actions: Check that the page identifies Tenable Nessus.
Leave activation-code and password boxes empty for now. We’ll handle those privately in the next lesson.
Bookmark this private HTTPS address with the scanner’s name so you can find it again.
steps.expected: The Nessus setup page is open. Nessus supplies this web interface itself; you do not need to install IIS.

screenshot.title: Identify the actual Nessus page — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the empty welcome/setup page before you type any activation information.

lessons.pass: Your Windows browser shows the Nessus setup page for the scanner you intended to open.
needs: Finish the service and firewall checks so Windows can reach TCP 8834 on the scanner.
Have the scanner’s private address and a trusted way to compare its initial certificate details. Open a browser on Windows.

lessons.title: Activate and Initialize Plugins
lessons.description: We’ll choose your licensed edition, create the scanner login and wait for its inspection checks to load.
lessons.what: Activation tells Nessus which edition you may use. Plugins are its inspection checklists—the individual checks it needs before it can scan.
lessons.why: A service can be running while the scanner is still getting ready. We’ll check the license route and plugin status instead of assuming it is ready just because a page opens.
bestPractices: Choose the edition and registration route your license actually permits. The installer alone does not unlock every scan template or feature.
Use a unique password for the Nessus administrator and save it in your approved password manager.
Keep activation codes, offline registration addresses and license text private. Enter them only in the correct Nessus or Tenable page, not in the academy.
commonMistakes: Nessus Essentials does not support offline installation. Choose a supported licensed route if the scanner will be offline.
Plugin loading can take longer than a few minutes. Read its status and check resources before deciding it has failed.

troubleshooting.problem: Activation or plugin loading fails online.
troubleshooting.fix: Check your edition and license, clock, DNS, available disk space and the allowed outbound HTTPS/proxy path. If you are building an offline scanner, use the next lesson’s offline process instead of trying online feed commands.

lessons.exercise: Write down the edition, installed version and plugin date you actually see. Explain what plugins do, but leave the activation code out of your notes.

quiz.question: What chooses which Nessus edition you may use?
options: Your valid entitlement and activation.
The number of screenshots in the class.
The VM name alone.
quiz.explanation: A single scanner package can serve editions; licensing determines access.

quiz.question: Can Essentials use the documented offline installation route?
options: Yes, with any tar.gz file.
No; the official offline-install page excludes Essentials.
Only if you install IIS.
quiz.explanation: Check license or evaluation permission before choosing an offline build.

steps.title: Choose the allowed setup route
steps.where: Physical Windows host · verified Nessus setup page
actions: On the verified Nessus setup page, choose the product type that matches your actual license or registration option.
For an online setup, follow that edition’s registration form and enter your valid activation information privately.
For a permitted offline Pro, Expert or Manager installation, choose Register Offline and follow the next lesson. Do not choose Essentials for an offline build.
steps.expected: The product and online/offline route match the license you have, rather than a feature you hope the installer includes.

screenshot.title: Choose the allowed setup route — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the edition-choice page before any activation code, license text or private feed address is visible.

steps.title: Create the scanner administrator privately
steps.where: Physical Windows host · Nessus setup page
actions: When prompted, create the Nessus administrator account. This is a login for the scanner; it is not automatically your Linux labadmin account.
Choose a unique strong password and put it in your password manager rather than your class notes.
Finish the form and let Nessus download and compile its plugins, or complete the supported offline import. Compiling means preparing the checks for use.
steps.expected: Nessus accepts the administrator setup and begins preparing its plugin set.

screenshot.title: Create the scanner administrator privately — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture a progress screen only after checking that no username, password or registration details are visible.

steps.title: Confirm initialization finished
steps.where: Physical Windows host · Nessus sign-in and settings
actions: Wait until the initialization page finishes, then sign in privately.
Open Settings → About/Software Update and check the product, installed version and plugin status. The labels may vary with edition.
If plugins are missing or still loading, pause before creating scans. Use the troubleshooting lesson to find out what is holding them up.
steps.expected: You can verify the licensed product, version 10.12.5 and a loaded plugin set on your own screen.

screenshot.title: Confirm initialization finished — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture just version and plugin status. Hide activation codes, account details and private update addresses.

lessons.pass: You can sign in to the intended edition, and plugin initialization has finished without an unresolved error.
needs: Open the verified Nessus setup page and know which edition and registration route your license permits.
Have your private activation details and password manager ready. Keep them off screenshots and shared notes.
For an offline build, check that the edition supports offline installation and use the next lesson for its matching files.

lessons.title: Handle Offline License and Signed Updates
lessons.description: If your scanner cannot use the internet, let’s check the license and signed update files it needs.
lessons.what: An offline scanner cannot download its own plugins. We use an allowed internet-connected computer to get the right files and bring them over through the lab’s approved transfer process.
lessons.why: Nessus 10.12.5 checks the signature on a manual plugin update. We need the correct archive and its matching trusted signature, not just a file with a convincing name.
bestPractices: Keep the license file, challenge code and private feed address protected. The license must be valid for this scanner and the edition you selected.
Get the official plugin archive and matching signature together from the permitted source. Renaming a different signature will not make it match.
Keep plugin updates separate from Nessus application updates. A plugin archive contains checks; it is not automatically a new application installer.
commonMistakes: nessus-updates-10.12.5.tar.gz by itself does not prove what is inside or meet the 10.12.5 signature requirement.
Your private license file and a plugin signature do different jobs. One cannot replace the other.

troubleshooting.problem: I have the archive but no matching signature.
troubleshooting.fix: Pause the import. Ask the license administrator for the correct Tenable archive/signature pair and confirm the archive’s purpose. We cannot safely finish this step with a guessed replacement.

lessons.exercise: Make a checklist of the required items without opening secrets: installer identified, edition confirmed, scanner-matching license available, plugin archive type verified and matching signature available.

quiz.question: What is mandatory for manual Nessus 10.12.5 plugin imports?
options: Only a file whose name ends in tar.gz.
A valid matching Tenable plugin signature as well as the archive.
An IIS website.
quiz.explanation: 10.12.5 added signature requirements for these manual plugin imports.

quiz.question: Can a filename prove the archive is a plugin update?
options: No; verify provenance, purpose and matching vendor artifacts.
Yes, if it contains the version number.
Yes, if it is copied over SCP.
quiz.explanation: Copying or renaming does not establish artifact type or trust.

steps.title: Identify the files before importing
steps.where: Windows host · private approved artifact inventory
actions: Look up where nessus-updates-10.12.5.tar.gz came from and read its vendor description or manifest. Find out whether it is a plugin archive, an application update or another kind of package.
Check that you also have its matching trusted signature file. The private license file is not that signature.
If you cannot confirm the file type or signature, write STOP — artifact verification needed in your notebook and do not run an update command yet.
steps.expected: Every file has a known job, and anything still unidentified has been left unused.

screenshot.title: Identify the files before importing — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture only the checklist of file roles and checks. Hide license contents and private download addresses.

steps.title: Use the scanner-bound offline license
steps.where: NESSUS-ALMA09 · offline setup and approved private registration computer
actions: For a new offline setup, choose Register Offline and get this scanner’s challenge code. Think of the challenge as part of the process for tying the license to this scanner.

On the allowed online computer, use Tenable’s official offline registration page with that challenge and valid activation entitlement. Transfer the resulting scanner license through the approved secure route.

For an existing scanner being changed to offline mode, use register-offline only after checking that the license belongs to this scanner and edition. Replace the sample file path with its protected local path.
steps.command:
sudo /opt/nessus/sbin/nessuscli fetch --challenge
# Existing scanner only; replace this path with its verified private license file:
sudo /opt/nessus/sbin/nessuscli fetch --register-offline /secure/path/nessus.license

breakdown.meaning: Installed Nessus administrator utility.
Shows the scanner-specific challenge for private offline registration.
Registers an existing scanner with its valid offline license and enables offline mode.
Placeholder for private approved storage, not a file supplied by this website.
A shell comment; the command below it is conditional, not something to run blindly.

steps.expected: Nessus accepts the matching offline license, or you stop at the mismatch. No license text needs to be stored in SONIC-Academy.

screenshot.title: Use the scanner-bound offline license — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: After registration, capture only a safely redacted offline/registered status. Never show the challenge, activation code, license text or private update address.

steps.title: Import only a verified signed plugin pair
steps.where: NESSUS-ALMA09 · Terminal or Nessus Software Update page
actions: Continue only after the plugin archive and signature are confirmed as the matching official pair for this scanner.
Replace both example paths in the command below. You may instead use Settings → Software Update → Manual Software Update → Upload your own plugin archive and signature file.

Let Nessus verify and initialize the files, then check the plugin status and date. If signature verification fails, save the error privately and stop; do not bypass it or switch to an unrelated online update command.
steps.command: sudo /opt/nessus/sbin/nessuscli update /path/to/plugins.tar.gz /path/to/plugins.tar.gz.sig

breakdown.meaning: Imports the explicitly supplied local update files.
Placeholder for the verified official Nessus plugin archive; not proof that your similarly named file has this role.
The matching trusted Tenable signature file required for these manual imports in10.12.5.

steps.expected: The verified import finishes and plugins load, or you keep the error and leave the scanner unchanged until the missing requirement is resolved.

screenshot.title: Import only a verified signed plugin pair — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the redacted update result and plugin date. Hide local paths if they reveal private storage.

lessons.pass: You either finish the supported offline setup with the correct license and signed plugin pair, or clearly record what is missing and leave the import paused.
needs: Use this lesson if your scanner must work without an internet connection; an online scanner follows its normal supported update route.
You’ll need an entitled offline edition, an allowed online registration computer, and a license that matches this scanner. Essentials does not support this route.
Before importing plugins, have the verified official plugin archive and its matching signature together. The name nessus-updates-10.12.5.tar.gz alone is not enough.

lessons.title: Troubleshoot Without Disabling Protection
lessons.description: If something is not working, let’s narrow it down one check at a time.
lessons.what: We’ll work through the service, its listening port, the network and the update route. A stopped application and a blocked connection need different fixes.
lessons.why: Following the clues helps us fix the real cause while leaving the firewall and SELinux protection in place.
bestPractices: Keep SELinux enforcing and firewall access narrow. If a policy needs changing, review a specific correction with the administrator first.
Keep logs private. Even an ordinary error log may contain machine names, addresses or scan information.
commonMistakes: Restarting repeatedly can interrupt work while leaving the real DNS, disk or license problem untouched.
Turning off the firewall or SELinux is not our shortcut for getting a page to load.

troubleshooting.fix: Check the service and listener on the VM first. Then check its active firewall zone, allowed source, private route and the Windows TCP test.
Check free disk space, memory, time, DNS, your edition and the chosen update route. Write down the actual error so we can choose the next check.
Read the specific denied action with your instructor. Test a narrow approved correction in a matching test VM; do not turn a broad allow-everything policy into the fix.

lessons.exercise: Choose a real error or one your instructor supplies. Explain your next diagnostic check and why it fits that error. We do not need to break a working scanner to practice reading clues.

quiz.question: The service is stopped. What should you inspect first?
options: Add every firewall port.
Service status and relevant logs.
Delete the license.
quiz.explanation: A firewall change cannot start a stopped service.

quiz.question: SELinux reports a denial. What is the right approach?
options: Disable SELinux permanently.
Ignore all errors.
Review the exact denial and a narrow tested policy correction.
quiz.explanation: Keep protection enabled and fix the specific cause.

steps.title: Read service and storage evidence
actions: At the scanner Terminal, run the service, log, disk and memory checks below.
Look for the first meaningful error. The last line may be a consequence rather than the cause.
Write down the time, error and free space for /opt, where Nessus stores its files. Keep full logs private rather than pasting them into a public issue.
steps.command:
sudo systemctl status nessusd --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u nessusd -b --no-pager -n 80
df -h /opt
free -h

breakdown.meaning: Reads log messages for the Nessus service, instead of mixing them with every other service.
Limits these log messages to the current boot of the VM.
Shows the newest 80 log entries, giving us a manageable place to start reading.
Shows human-readable free space for the filesystem holding /opt, where Nessus keeps its files.
Shows available and used memory in readable units such as GiB.

steps.expected: You can tell whether the service failed and whether a useful error, full disk or resource shortage points to the cause.

screenshot.title: Read service and storage evidence — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the relevant redacted service error and disk-space line, not a whole private log.

steps.title: Separate local application and network tests
steps.where: NESSUS-ALMA09 console, then Windows host PowerShell
actions: On Linux, check the TCP 8834 listener and firewall rules using the commands below.
On Windows, repeat Test-NetConnection using the scanner’s current private address and port 8834.
If the IP works but the name does not, look at DNS. If the TCP test works but the browser warns, look at the certificate. Do not widen the firewall to solve a certificate warning.
steps.command:
sudo ss -lntp 'sport = :8834'

steps.title: Investigate SELinux carefully
actions: Check the SELinux mode and recent access-denial messages. SELinux is an extra set of rules about what programs may do.
If sealert is missing, install the approved AlmaLinux setroubleshoot-server package before trying its report command. On an offline machine, use the approved package/dependency plan.

Read the exact denied operation with your instructor. Try a narrow approved correction in a matching test VM, restart only when needed, and check again. Do not apply a broad policy without understanding it.
steps.command:
getenforce
sudo ausearch -m AVC,USER_AVC -ts recent
# If approved repositories are available and sealert is missing:
sudo dnf install setroubleshoot-server
sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log

breakdown.meaning: Shows whether SELinux is enforcing its protection rules, permissive or disabled.
Searches Linux’s audit log for the kinds of messages you ask for.
Selects SELinux access-denial message types.
Limits the audit search to recent events so we start with the messages most likely to relate to our test.
Analyzes the named audit log and offers diagnostic guidance; review recommendations, do not blindly apply them.
The system audit log path; keep it private.
Installs the approved AlmaLinux package that supplies sealert; an offline host needs an approved dependency/media plan instead of an internet repository.

steps.expected: SELinux stays enforcing. You either find no related denial or have a specific issue written down for review.

steps.title: Check the right update route
steps.where: NESSUS-ALMA09 · Nessus settings and private notes
actions: Check whether this scanner is configured for online or offline updates, and note its product and version.
For an online scanner, check DNS, time and the permitted outbound HTTPS port 443/proxy route. For an offline scanner, check its matching license and signed plugin pair.
Write down the exact error and what requirement must be fixed before you retry. Leave activation codes, license text, passwords and private feed addresses out of shared notes.
steps.expected: Your proposed next step fits the scanner’s actual update route and keeps signature checks in place.

lessons.title: Prove the Scanner Is Ready
lessons.description: Let’s put the checks together and make sure your scanner is really ready.
lessons.what: We’ll check several parts of the setup: the installed package, the running service, browser access, activation and plugins. One green light is useful; the full chain is more convincing.
lessons.why: It is easy to mistake an open welcome page for a finished installation. These checks help us spot anything still missing before the scanning class.
bestPractices: Record what your own screen shows and when you checked it. An example in a course is not saved result from your VM.
A ready scanner still needs a permitted target list, a reviewed scan policy and a credential plan before it scans anything.
commonMistakes: An active service does not tell us whether plugins finished loading.
The welcome page can appear before activation is complete, so it is only one part of our check.

troubleshooting.fix: That tells us which part needs more attention. Leave the installation incomplete, return to that lesson, make a documented correction and repeat the check. You do not need to redo a working step just to fill a page.

lessons.exercise: Give a two-minute handoff: show each readiness check and explain what it proves. Keep the license and passwords out of the demonstration.

quiz.question: Which set best proves installation readiness?
options: Only a ping reply.
Version, service/listener, private browser access, entitlement and loaded plugins.
Only the downloaded RPM filename.
quiz.explanation: Readiness spans package, service, connectivity and application initialization.

quiz.question: Should you mark the lab ready if plugins are still initializing?
options: No; wait or diagnose until plugin readiness is verified.
Yes, as soon as the VM starts.
Yes, if the firewall is disabled.
quiz.explanation: The scanner needs usable plugins before the next administration lab.

steps.title: Verify package and service together
actions: Ask the package manager which Nessus version is installed by running the first command below.
Check whether nessusd is enabled for boot and active right now. These are two separate questions.
Compare your results with the plan. We are looking for your actual installed version and service state, not a value copied from a lesson.
steps.command:
rpm -q Nessus
systemctl is-enabled nessusd
systemctl is-active nessusd

breakdown.meaning: Asks the installed-package record which Nessus version is on this machine.
Asks whether Linux is set to start the service during boot; it does not prove it is running now.
Asks whether the service is running at this moment; it does not start a stopped service.

steps.expected: Your VM reports the expected Nessus 10.12.5 package, and the service has the intended boot and current running states.

screenshot.title: Verify package and service together — capture needed
screenshot.instructions: Capture the real package and service checks from the scanner Terminal.

steps.title: Verify private console and plugin readiness
actions: On Windows, open your bookmarked private HTTPS address and sign in to Nessus.
In Settings, check the product edition, installed version and plugin date/status. Wait if initialization is still running.
Review the management firewall rule too. It should name the allowed source, rather than expose the page to every address.
steps.expected: You can reach the intended private console, and plugin initialization is finished for your licensed edition.

steps.title: Write the non-secret handoff
actions: In your notebook, record the scanner name and IP, AlmaLinux version and architecture, Nessus version, activation route, plugin date and the date you checked readiness.
Write down the management rule and who is responsible for keeping certificates and updates healthy.
List any unresolved issue honestly. If it prevents scanning, leave the lab incomplete so the next person knows what still needs work.
steps.expected: Someone else could find this scanner and understand its maintenance plan without receiving your passwords in the handoff.

needs: Have the installed scanner running, with its configured license route and plugins ready.
Open Linux Terminal and your Windows browser, and keep your installation and firewall notes nearby. We’ll compare several checks together.

lessons.title: Finish the AlmaLinux Installation Lab
lessons.description: Your turn: show the scanner working and explain how you would look after it.
lessons.what: We’ll use your own results to walk through the finished setup. The goal is to explain what you built, not just show that you copied a command.
lessons.why: At work, another person may need to support the scanner after you. A clear demonstration and handoff make that much easier.
bestPractices: Treat Nessus backups as private: they can contain settings and license information. Use Tenable’s backup procedure and approved protected storage.
Do not clone an activated scanner identity to make another scanner. Use the documented licensing and migration process when rebuilding or moving it.
Do not run fetch --security-center just to demonstrate an ACAS term. It changes the scanner’s management mode.
commonMistakes: A capture placeholder asks for a real screenshot; it does not prove that a lab step succeeded.
Keep practice targets separate from production. We do not need to weaken a work server to learn scanning.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot explain a command I used.
troubleshooting.fix: That is a useful place to pause. Open its command breakdown, name the computer where it runs, and practice a safe read-only check before continuing.

lessons.exercise: Demonstrate NESSUS-ALMA09, its restricted HTTPS page and its readiness checks. Explain activation and the signed offline-update rule, then hand over notes without secrets. We’ll launch target scans in Class 03, after its preparation steps.

quiz.question: What should your final evidence contain?
options: Your complete license and password.
Only the course’s placeholder image.
Your own sanitized version, service, firewall, console and plugin checks.
quiz.explanation: Saved result comes from the actual lab and excludes secrets.

quiz.question: What comes before scanning the target VMs?
options: A reviewed scope, approved targets, policy and credential plan in Class03.
Opening every inbound port on the scanner.
Converting the scanner to Security Center management.
quiz.explanation: Installation readiness does not replace authorization and scan configuration.

lessons.pass: You have completed the installation and knowledge checks using real private saved result, and you have a permitted two-target plan ready for the scanning class.
needs: Bring your working NESSUS-ALMA09 scanner and the real saved result collected in earlier lessons.
Have your permitted two-target plan ready for the next class; the scanner itself must remain separate from those target VMs.
Keep the license, private keys and passwords protected while you demonstrate the non-secret checks.

supplies: Use a Windows computer with VMware Workstation Pro. It needs enough spare resources for the scanner and the target VMs while Windows keeps running.

For our scanner VM, plan 4 virtual CPU cores, 8 GB RAM and a new 80 GB virtual disk. RAM is working memory; the disk keeps files after shutdown. These are our teaching allocations, not a guarantee for every workload.

Download a supported AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 ISO from the official project. An ISO acts like an installation disc; x86_64 is for 64-bit Intel/AMD processors. Tenable’s current support table lists AlmaLinux 9.6 and later in the 9.x family.
Have Nessus-10.12.5-el9.x86_64.rpm from Tenable ready on Windows. This RPM is the Linux installation package for the Nessus scanner; it is not the Nessus Agent installer.
Use the private VMware lab network from the network-setup lesson and keep a notebook of its actual addresses. We’ll keep the scanner separate from the AlmaLinux and Windows computers it will inspect.

Have a valid Nessus registration option or license for your chosen edition. If the scanner must work offline, check that the edition supports it and get the matching scanner license, plugin archive and signature; Nessus Essentials does not support offline installation.
